AK-2025-HJR20.aiSummary: The Alaska Legislature adopted a resolution that asks Congress to set hiring goals for apprentices and veteran apprentices on U.S. Defense Department construction projects in the United States. It would call for at least 20 percent of the workforce on those projects to be in apprenticeship or postsecondary programs. It would also call for at least 10 percent of those apprentices or students in each job class to be veterans.

AK-2025-HB93.aiSummary: The bill would change the residency rules for hunting, trapping, and sport fishing privileges in Alaska. It would require people with a permanent ID card to still meet the state’s resident rules, and it would update the rules for who counts as a resident when applying for a license. The state fish and game commissioner would also have to set rules for checking if someone qualifies as a resident, and the law would take effect on January 1, 2028.

AK-2025-HB16.aiSummary: The bill would require some groups that support or oppose a candidate or ballot measure in Alaska elections to keep a physical address in the state or use an in-state agent. It would raise campaign donation limits for state and local offices, and the Alaska Public Offices Commission would adjust those limits every 10 years starting in 2031 based on inflation. It would also change reporting and complaint rules for election complaints, and it would set rules for spending and donations by foreign-influenced corporations and foreign nationals.

AK-2025-HB388.aiSummary: This law raises the loan limit from Alaska’s bulk fuel loan account and bulk fuel bridge loan account to $1.5 million per borrower. For some cooperative groups that buy fuel for more than one community, the bulk fuel loan amount can be multiplied by the number of communities served. It also lets the state use money from the bulk fuel revolving loan fund to cover these loans in fiscal years 2026 and 2027 if the fund balance is not enough, and it took effect on July 3, 2026.

AK-2025-SB239.aiSummary: Signed into law in Alaska, this act changes rules for some commercial driver license tests, imported vehicles, and proof of financial responsibility after a judgment. It lets a driver who fails part of a driving test retake only the part they missed. For vehicles at least 25 years old that were legally imported, the state could register and title them without making them meet current federal safety standards, and insurance customers with certain judgment-related suspensions would have new time periods for keeping proof on file.
